purpose: Pegfilgrastim-apgf is used to help your body make more white blood cells after you receive chemotherapy for cancer. Chemotherapy can lower your white blood cell count, which makes it harder for your body to fight infections. This medicine helps reduce your risk of getting serious infections during your cancer treatment.
how_it_works: Your bone marrow is like a factory that makes blood cells. This medicine acts like a natural signal in your body called G-CSF, which tells your bone marrow to produce more white blood cells called neutrophils. More neutrophils means your immune system is better equipped to fight off bacteria and other germs.
common_side_effects: The most common side effect is bone or muscle aching, especially in the lower back, hips, or legs. You might also feel tired, have headaches, or notice mild redness or soreness where the injection was given. Some people feel nausea or joint pain as well.
warnings: Call your doctor right away if you have serious bone pain, difficulty breathing, a fast heartbeat, or pain in the upper left belly or left shoulder, as this could be a sign of a rare but serious problem with your spleen. This medicine should not be given between 14 days before and 24 hours after chemotherapy. Tell your doctor if you have sickle cell disease, as this medicine can cause complications.
typical_dosing: This medicine is given as a single injection under the skin (subcutaneous) once per chemotherapy cycle. The usual adult dose is 6 mg, given about 24 hours after your chemotherapy is finished. Your nurse or doctor will give it to you, or you may be taught to give it at home using a prefilled syringe or an on-body injector device.
